# Secondary Data {.unnumbered}

Secondary data refers to data that has been collected by someone other than CCDPH and is therefore not originally generated by the Epidemiology Unit for a specific purpose. These data can include state (e.g., IDPH) and federal (e.g., from the CDC, Census Bureau, or EPA) government datasets, and many other sources. The Epidemiology Unit uses secondary data to develop public health indicators, and explore relationships between various social, economic, and environmental phenomena. This section briefly summarizes key secondary data sources used by the Epidemiology Unit and provides links to in-depth processing instructions.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false

library(DBI)
library(odbc)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(DT)
library(keyring)
library(stringr)
library(openxlsx)
library(data.table)
library(sf)
```

## Vital statistics
Vital statistics refer to the systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of data related to key life events such as births and deaths, including maternal and fetal deaths. Vital statistics provide critical information about the health of a population. Epidemiologists and public health professionals use vital statistics to track and understand health outcomes. In Illinois, vital records are collected, maintained and distributed by the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) and made available to local health departments including the Cook County Department of Public Health. The vital records received by CCDPH from IDPH include specific information including the residential location of individuals who reside(d) within suburban Cook County. These data are crucial for understanding and monitoring mortality patterns and trends. When stratified by factors such as age, sex, race/ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, the data allows CCDPH epidemiologists to identify disparities in health outcomes and help inform interventions accordingly. Code for collaborating on the processing of vital statistics data irsts managed via the [ccdph-vital-statistics](https://github.com/Cook-County-Department-of-Public-Health/ccdph-vital-statistics) GitHub repository. Links to detailed instructions for processing birth and death records are available via the following links:

### Mortality, death certificate data
Background and purpose. CCDPH manages vital statistics mortality (death certificate) data obtained from IDPH under the same DUA framework used for natality data, with data requests coordinated through designated staff and Director sign-off. Death certificate records capture decedent demographics, date and place of death, cause of death, and certifying-physician information, and support CCDPH public health research, resource allocation, and mortality surveillance. Indicators cover a broad set of chronic disease, injury, and other non-communicable causes of death — including all/site-specific cancers (lung, colorectal, pancreatic, breast, cervical, uterine, ovarian, prostate, and a screenable-cancers composite), diabetes, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, hypertension, stroke, respiratory disease, chronic liver disease, nephritis, and injury/external causes (unintentional injury, suicide, homicide, falls, firearms, drug poisoning/overdose, and transport-related deaths), plus compound indicators such as drug-, alcohol-, and tobacco-induced deaths. Infectious/parasitic diseases (ICD-10 Chapter I) and COVID-19 are explicitly excluded, as these fall under the CCDPH Communicable Disease Unit. Data processing is organized in four phases.

* [Phase One](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/Phase_01_mortality_data.html) covers acquisition and geocoding: fixed-width death files and IDPH data dictionaries are downloaded to the network drive, imported into epi-vitals by year, quality-checked (e.g., standardizing non-conforming column names such as the 2015 file), and transformed into a formatted multi-year table with CCDPH-standard race/ethnicity, age group, ICD-10-based cause-of-death, and geography variables. Records are geocoded via the Cook County locator (IDPH-supplied coordinates being unreliable) and spatially joined to census tracts (2010 and 2020 vintages), ZCTAs, and municipalities, with cumulative tables appended server-side to control memory use. 

* [Phase Two](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/Phase_02_mortality_data.html) classifies each death into binary (0/1) ICD-10-CM-based condition indicators using a centralized reference table, then aggregates counts and calculates crude and age-adjusted rates (using SEER 2000 standard population weights and annualized decennial population denominators) across geography (SCC, CCDPH jurisdiction, health region, municipality, ZCTA), race/ethnicity, sex, and broad age group, producing both single-year and five-year rolling pooled indicator tables. 

* [Phase Three](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/Phase_03_mortality_data.html) applies IDPH's Aggregate Data Suppression Policy: counts of 1–9 are suppressed unless the geography's population exceeds 20,000 (exempting SCC/CCDPH/region-level data), and rates/AARs are suppressed when the underlying count is under 20; municipality and ZCTA layers apply both thresholds directly since their populations are frequently below the exemption cutoff. 

* [Phase Four](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/Phase_04_mortality_data.html) formats the suppressed indicator tables for downstream dissemination — building Metopio-convention column names and annual CSV extracts for the Cook County Health Atlas (split to respect the platform's 1,000-column upload limit), an Excel workbook of leading causes of death by race/ethnicity for CCDPH Communications, and a formatted extract for the Cook County Open Data Portal.

### Natality, birth certificate data
CCDPH manages vital statistics natality (birth certificate) data obtained from the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) under a signed data use agreement (DUA), with data requests routed through designated staff and Director approval required for access. These records support core maternal and child health (MCH) indicators — including crude birth rate, general fertility rate, teenage and early-teen birth rates, multiple births, birth weight and cesarean delivery, infant mortality, parental demographics, prenatal care adequacy (via the Kotelchuck APNCU Index), gestational diabetes/hypertension, smoking during pregnancy, breastfeeding at discharge, and very preterm birth — calculated across geographies (suburban Cook County, CCDPH jurisdiction, health region, municipality, and ZCTA) and, where feasible, stratified by race/ethnicity and maternal age. These indicators inform CCDPH public health research, policy development, resource allocation, and public dissemination through the Cook County Health Atlas. Data management proceeds in two phases documented in companion Quarto workflow files within the ccdph-vital-statistics GitHub repository. 

* [Phase One](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/Phase_01_natality_data.html) covers acquisition through geocoding: raw fixed-width birth files and IDPH data dictionaries are saved to the Epi Unit's network drive, imported into the epi-vitals SQL Server database by year (raw.births_scc_YYYY), consolidated into a formatted multi-year table with standardized race/ethnicity and age-group categorization, and geocoded before being spatially joined to census tracts, ZCTAs, municipalities, and health regions. 

* [Phase Twp](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/Phase_02_natality_data.html) covers indicator calculation and dissemination: binary 0/1 indicator flags are created per birth record, aggregated into count and rate tables using population and live-birth denominators (with five-year rolling aggregation at the municipal/ZCTA level to reduce suppression needs), and finally suppressed and formatted per DUA rules — removing direct identifiers, masking non-zero counts under 5 and rates derived from counts under 20 (with higher thresholds for sensitive topics), and favoring aggregation over suppression where possible — before export to the Health Atlas. A separate live births count indicator (total, by race/ethnicity, and by maternal age group) is calculated additively across all five geographies and years (2010–2024) using the same suppression and formatting conventions. Mortality-based MCH indicators (infant and maternal mortality) are documented separately in the mortality data processing section of this handbook.

### Life expectancy
Life expectancy is a statistical measure of the average number of years a person born in a specific year could expect to live, assuming that age-specific death rates remain constant throughout their lifetime. The calculation uses abridged life tables constructed from age-specific death rates (estimated from death certificate vital statistics data) applied to population data, following the Chiang methodology. Age groups conform to the standard abridged structure: 0, 1, 5–9, 10–14, … 85–89, and 90+. For age groups with no recorded deaths, a substituted value of 0.5 is used to ensure numerical stability.

* Refer to the [Life expectancy calculations](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/life_expectancy.html) document for information about this indicator as well as the steps for processing and disseminating. 

### Years of potential life lost
Years of Potential Life Lost (YPLL) is a summary measure of premature mortality used widely in public health surveillance. Rather than simply counting deaths or calculating a crude or age-adjusted death rate, YPLL estimates the number of years someone would have been expected to live had they not died before a defined age threshold -- commonly age 65 or 75. For each death occurring before that threshold, YPLL is calculated as the difference between the threshold age and the decedent's age at death; deaths that occur at or after the threshold contribute zero years to the measure. This script uses a threshold of 75 years, consistent with common national and state public health reporting standards.

* Refer to the [Years of potential life lost](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/ypll.html) document for information about this indicator as well as the steps for processing and disseminating. 

## Hospital discharge data
Hospital discharge data are administrative data collected when a patient is discharged from a hospital. Inpatient data is collected on patients admitted to a hospital for an overnight stay, while outpatient data is collected on patients who receive services from a hospital but do not stay overnight. The CCDPH receives both [inpatient and outpatient data](https://dph.illinois.gov/topics-services/prevention-wellness/patient-safety-quality/discharge-data.html) from the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) on an irregular basis. The discharge data include patient demographic information, diagnosis codes, procedures codes, charges, among other data. Code for collaborating on the processing of hospital discharge data is managed via the [ccdph-hospital-discharge](https://github.com/Cook-County-Department-of-Public-Health/ccdph-hospital-discharge) GitHub repository. Detailed instructions for processing hospital discharge data are available via the following link:

* [Steps for requesting, importing, cleaning, coding and transforming inpatient and outpatient hospital discharge data](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/hospital_discharge_latest_process.html)

## Emergency Medical Services (EMS) Data 
EMS data have the potential to give CCDPH a real-time look at what is happening in the community at the point of emergency response. These records come from electronic patient care reports completed by paramedics during 911 calls and follow national data standards set by the [National Emergency Medical Services Information System (NEMSIS)](https://nemsis.org/), which was created to standardize EMS data collection and improve data quality, comparability, and system performance nationwide. Because EMS data capture events at the scene—before hospital admission or death—they provide early insight into overdoses, mental health crises, suicide attempts, asthma attacks, diabetic emergencies, cardiac events, and other acute episodes tied to behavioral health and chronic disease. Compared to hospital discharge data (which reflect treated inpatient cases) and vital records (which reflect deaths), EMS data are more immediate and capture a broader range of community-level events, including those that may never result in hospitalization. Code for collaborating on the processing of EMS data is managed via the [ccdph-ems](https://github.com/Cook-County-Department-of-Public-Health/ccdph-ems) GitHub repository. Detailed instructions for processing EMS data are available via the following link:

* [Steps for requesting, importing, cleaning, coding and transforming EMS data](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/ems_data_processing_latest.html)


## Population data from the US Census Bureau
CCDPH epidemiologists rely on US Census data as demographic denominators to calculate public health metrics such as incidence, prevalence, mortality rates, and other key indicators. To calculate incidence and prevalence rates, CCDPH epidemiological staff needs to know the size of the population at risk. US Census data provides detailed population counts and demographic breakdowns by age, gender, race and ethnicity for multiple geographies including suburban Cook County, CCDPH's jurisdiction, health districts, municipalities, zip code tabulation areas (ZCTAs), and census tracts. Similarly, mortality rates (deaths per 1,000 or 100,000 people) require population data from the census to ensure accurate comparisons across different groups. Without census data, public health metrics would lack the context needed to interpret raw health event counts.

Census data is also used by CCDPH epidemiologists to standardize rates to account for differences in population structure. For example, older populations may have higher mortality rates simply because they have more elderly people. Age-adjusted rates, which use census age distribution, enable more accurate comparisons between populations with different age structures. Annualized US decennial census data is used to calculate population trends over time. By comparing health outcomes over time, epidemiologists can track changes in disease rates, mortality, or health behaviors in the context of population growth, aging, or migration.

Code for collaborating on the processing of census data is managed via the [ccdph-data-sets](https://github.com/Cook-County-Department-of-Public-Health/ccdph-data-sets) GitHub repository. Links to detailed instructions for processing American Community Survey (ACS) and decennial census data are available via the following links:

* [Steps for producing annualized population estimates by age, race, sex, SCC, CCDPH, MUNI, 2010-2022](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/annualized-population-2010-2022-10yr-age-race-sex-scc-ccdph-muni.html)
* [Steps for producing annualized population estimates by sex, ZCTA, 2010-2022](https://justenvirons.org/epihandbook/in_depth/annualized-population-2010-2022-10yr-age-female-zcta.html)
